..
Issued at 1018 PM CDT Mon Sep 7 2026

Tonight and Tuesday...

Water vapor imagery and objective analysis late this evening depicts 
a mid-level ridge centered over the southern and central Plains 
while a deepening cut-off low tracks eastward across 
Montana/Alberta. A weak surface front draped from central Nebraska 
into southeastern South Dakota has served as a focus for 
thunderstorm development earlier this evening. A modestly unstable 
airmass with steep mid-level lapse rates is in place over northeast 
Nebraska, though deep-layer shear remains rather limited (around
25 kts). However, a 35-40 kt LLJ in place has allowed for some 
hodograph curvature and enough low-level shear for initial storm
organization with a supercell that tracked over northeast 
Nebraska into southeast South Dakota before growing into more of
a messy, upscale cluster. With this in mind, a strong storm or 
two swiping across northeast Nebraska can't be ruled out, though
that chance will decrease through the overnight period as 
stability increases. Scattered showers and storm will persist 
and slowly sag southward into Tuesday morning as low-level 
moisture transport and WAA continues to point into the area. 

Tuesday, the aforementioned northern low will push a northeast-to-
southwest oriented trailing cold front into the area. High 
temperatures will depend on how far south the front progresses 
before peak daytime heating. High temperatures are expected to reach 
the mid to upper 90s across southeast NE and southwest IA. 
Continued low- level moisture transport ahead of the front will 
bring dewpoints into the low to mid 70s, pushing heat index 
values into the 104-108 degree range, generally along and south 
of Interstate-80 where a Heat Advisory is in place. Further 
north, highs are expected to peak in the mid 80s thanks to the 
passing front and continued showers/cloud cover.

Storm chances increase along the slowly advancing front Tuesday 
afternoon and evening as it passes through an increasing unstable 
airmass. While large scale forcing for ascent remains rather weak, 
there should be enough convergence along the front for convective 
initiation. Shear will be the limiting factor, with around 20-25 kts 
of bulk shear, limiting overall storm organization. Model soundings 
indicate fairly dry low-levels and DCAPE values approaching 1000 
J/kg, which could help to promote severe weather gusts (60-70 mph) 
with any storms that quickly pulse up and collapse. Pocket of hail 
(up to 1.50") also can't be ruled out given the modestly steep
low-level lapse rates in place. Into the evening and overnight 
period, attention will shift to heavy rainfall as training 
storms persist behind the front, generally along and south of 
I-80, brining repeated rounds of rainfall. Storms will be 
efficient rain producers, with PWAT values approaching 2 inches
(near the daily maximum of sounding climatology) and warm cloud
depths of 4-4.5 km. CAM guidance suggests pockets of 2-3+" 
before showers gradually taper off from north to south through 
Wednesday morning. 

Wednesday and Beyond...

The passing disturbance to the north will help to dampen the ridge 
that has dominated the region with above-average temperatures 
through the beginning of September. As a result, zonal flow will 
return to the area and drop highs on Wednesday and Thursday into the 
upper 70s to low 80s. On Friday, a brief mid-level ridge will pull a 
warm front northward across the area and allow highs to climb back 
into the mid to upper 80s. The warmer temperatures won't last long, 
as a passing disturbance will push a cold front back across the area 
into Saturday, dropping highs into the upper 70s to mid 80s, while 
also bringing PoPs of 40-60%. 

Looking further ahead, long-range guidance is coming into consensus 
on bringing a mid-level low across the northern Plains late next 
weekend into the early work week. This system is expected to bring 
another round of 30-50% PoPs as well as a push of CAA into the 
region, dropping high temperatures into the 70s for most 
locations, with a few spots potentially peaking in the upper 60s
Monday and Tuesday. For reference, the last time Omaha's high 
temperature peaked below 70 degrees was May 21st.
